opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly my answer has shifted a fair bit over the last few years.

When I first got into this, the bottleneck felt very conceptual. We didn't really know what the problems were, so what you most wanted were people who could think carefully about threat models: how might a system end up pursuing goals we didn't intend, what would deceptive alignment actually look like, that kind of thing. That work still matters, and I don't want to undersell it, but I think the balance has moved quite a lot toward empirical and engineering skills.

The reason is that we now have systems capable enough that many of these questions can actually be studied. You can run experiments on frontier models. You can try to elicit worrying behaviours, build model organisms of misalignment, test whether a monitoring setup catches things, and see whether interpretability tools tell you anything useful about what's going on inside. All of that is very bottlenecked on people who can run experiments quickly and rigorously, who are comfortable with large codebases and big training and evaluation infrastructure, and who have good taste about which experiment will actually change their minds.

So if I had to name the scarcest skill on the team, it's probably something like strong research engineering combined with good research judgement. That means someone who can take a somewhat fuzzy safety concern, turn it into a concrete experiment, execute it well, and then interpret the results honestly, including noticing when the result doesn't mean what you hoped it meant. Pure engineering talent without that judgement can produce a lot of output that doesn't move the needle. Pure conceptual talent without the ability to test ideas can end up going in circles.

Another skill I've come to value more is what you might call working well within a large organisation. At a place like Google DeepMind, a lot of the impact of safety work comes from it actually being adopted, whether that's in how models get evaluated before deployment, in frontier safety policies, or in what mitigations get built into training. That requires people who can communicate clearly with teams whose main job isn't safety, understand their constraints, and make the case for why something is worth doing. It's less glamorous than discovering some new alignment technique, but it's often where the rubber meets the road.

And then there's a smaller but still important need for people who can do the big-picture strategic thinking: figuring out what our overall approach should be, where the gaps are, and how the pieces fit together into something you'd actually want to rely on as systems get more capable. You don't need a huge number of those people, but having none would be bad.

So if someone listening is wondering how to be useful, my rough advice is: get really good at running experiments on ML systems, develop your own views about which safety problems matter and why, and practise explaining your work to people who aren't already bought in. That combination is pretty rare and pretty valuable right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the balance has shifted toward empirical and engineering skills, but it does not compare software engineering with machine learning research or specify a shift over the past year or two.

r002.rationale: It explains that capable systems can now be studied through experiments and evaluations, which makes research judgment relevant alongside research engineering and implementation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's shifted quite a bit over the last couple of years, and probably in a direction that surprises people who've been following the field from the outside.

If you'd asked me this four or five years ago, I would have said the bottleneck was pretty clearly conceptual work. Like, we didn't really know what problem we were solving, we had these somewhat vague worries about mesa-optimisers and deceptive alignment, and it felt like the most valuable thing a person could do was sit down and think hard about what alignment even means and what the threat models actually are. And I still think that work matters. But I don't think it's the main thing we're short on anymore.

What's happened is that the models have gotten good enough that most of the questions we care about have become empirical questions. You can actually go and test whether a model is sandbagging on dangerous capability evals. You can look at whether chain of thought is faithful to what the model is actually doing. You can build a monitor and see whether it catches the thing you want it to catch. And so the skills that are most in demand on the team now look a lot more like really strong ML engineering and really strong experimental research taste, rather than philosophy or theory.

And I'd actually break that down a bit further. There are roughly three profiles we end up needing a lot of.

The first is people who are just very good at running experiments on frontier models. That's partly infrastructure, partly knowing how to design an experiment so the result actually tells you something, and partly having the stamina to iterate quickly when the first five things you try don't work. This is probably the single biggest category.

The second is a more interpretability-flavoured skill set, people who can get inside the model and tell you something about what's going on mechanistically. That's still a smaller group, and it's more speculative, but I think the payoff if it works is pretty large, and frankly it's also where some of our best safety cases could come from eventually.

And the third, which I think is underrated, is what I'd loosely call the "safety case" or "red teaming and evaluation" skill set. People who can think adversarially about how a mitigation could fail, who can take a fuzzy argument like "we think the model isn't capable of X" and turn it into something that's actually legible to a decision maker. That's a bit of a hybrid of research and something closer to security engineering or even policy. And it's surprisingly hard to find people who are good at it, because it requires being rigorous without being the kind of person who gets paralysed by every edge case.

Where I think we're relatively less bottlenecked, and this might be controversial, is on pure conceptual alignment research in the sense of writing long documents about what the problem is. Not because it's unimportant, but because I think we have a reasonable amount of it relative to our ability to actually act on it. The constraint is turning ideas into things that can be tested and deployed.

One more thing I'd add is that as the team has grown, there's a very real need for people who can do the connective tissue work. Someone who can talk to the pretraining team, understand what their constraints actually are, and figure out how to get a safety intervention into a real production model without it being a massive fight. That is a real skill, and it's not the sort of thing that shows up on a CV, but it's often the difference between research that ends up in a paper and research that ends up in the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from conceptual alignment work toward ML engineering and experimental research, but does not say software engineering is emphasized relative to machine learning research.

r002.rationale: It says safety questions are now empirical and can be tested on models, and identifies experimental research skills as in demand alongside engineering. This connects evaluation of systems to research-oriented work.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is that we need a mix of research judgment and strong engineering. A lot of the work involves taking a fairly vague concern about future AI systems and turning it into something we can actually study today. What experiment would tell us whether this is a real problem? If we tried a mitigation, how would we know it had worked, rather than just made the problem harder to detect?

That requires people who can think carefully about the alignment problem, but it also requires people who can build reliable experiments and work effectively with models. And those aren’t necessarily different people. Someone who can move between the conceptual question and the implementation is particularly valuable.

I’d be hesitant to give a precise ratio, because it depends on which projects we’re pursuing. But I wouldn’t think of it as needing only people with novel ideas about alignment. There’s a lot of value in making an idea concrete, testing it carefully, and figuring out what the result actually tells us.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a mix of research judgment and engineering, but gives no comparison with a year or two earlier and does not say engineering has gained emphasis relative to machine learning research.

r002.rationale: It says research judgment remains necessary to frame questions and assess whether experiments or mitigations worked, alongside building reliable experiments and working with models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the balance has shifted somewhat towards people who can do really good empirical research with current models. We have systems now where you can actually try an alignment technique, see where it fails, and iterate. So having people who are strong at machine learning, who can design informative experiments and get them working, is very valuable.

But I wouldn’t want a team composed entirely of people optimising the next experiment. You also need people asking, “Why should we expect this approach to work as models become much more capable? What assumptions are we making, and how could those assumptions break?” Otherwise you can end up making progress on something measurable without making progress on the problem you ultimately care about.

And then there’s an engineering component: making it easy to run experiments, evaluate models, and build on each other’s work. Those skills can have a lot of leverage across the team.

So I don’t think there’s one ideal profile that everyone should fit. I’m more interested in having a mixture, with people who can communicate across those different strengths. The conceptual questions should inform the experiments, and the experiments should change how we think about the conceptual questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate says emphasis has shifted toward empirical research with current models and mentions engineering as valuable, but does not state that software engineering now outweighs machine learning research or compare the balance with a year or two earlier.

r002.rationale: It says current systems let researchers try alignment techniques, see where they fail, and iterate, explaining why empirical research and experiment-design skills remain valuable in implementation-focused work.
